passage: Vikas had been a clerk at the cooperative bank in Sirsi for exactly one month, and on the 22nd his phone showed a balance that wouldn't cover the bus pass. "Where did it go?" he asked Chaitanya at the tea stall outside the bank. "I bought one thing. The shoes." Chaitanya took the phone and scrolled through the payment history slowly, the way the bank had taught them to check a ledger. Shoes, once. Then the evening snack order from the delivery app, nineteen times. A video subscription, a music subscription and a cricket-streaming pass he'd forgotten about. Chai and samosa, almost daily. Two mobile recharges. "The shoes aren't your problem," Chaitanya said. "This is." He tapped the long column of small amounts. Vikas stared at it. Not one of them had felt like spending. Together they looked like the whole salary.

qa.q: How many times had Vikas ordered the evening snack from the delivery app?
qa.a: Nineteen times.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel looking at the long column of small amounts?
qa.a: He was confused and dismayed, since he had blamed the shoes and none of the small payments had felt like spending.

qa.q: What could Vikas do before next month's salary is gone?
qa.a: He could go through the list with Chaitanya, stop the subscriptions he had forgotten, and keep an eye on the small daily payments as they happen.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see the problem?
qa.a: Chaitanya sees it plainly and kindly, checking the history like a ledger and pointing out that the pile of small amounts matters more than the one big buy.

grounding: Shows a first-job earner who runs out of money before the month ends and discovers that small repeated orders and forgotten subscriptions, not one purchase, used it up.

subtype: Easy credit and buy now pay later [Actor]
passage: The student help desk in the university library basement was quiet at four, and Zainab slid her phone across to Jomon, the volunteer. "There's a late charge on this and I don't understand why." Jomon opened the three pay-later apps she pointed to, one by one, and wrote on a notepad. Headphones in March, "no-cost", six instalments. A winter jacket in April, pay in three. Concert tickets for her and her roommate. A phone cover. Each one had felt tiny. "I thought no-cost meant free," she said quietly. Jomon added up the column and turned the pad towards her. Her eyes widened. The monthly total was more than her part-time library wages. Two instalments had gone unpaid during exam week, and the late fees had stacked on top. "Okay," Jomon said. "Don't panic. Let's book you in with the college's finance advisor on Thursday, and bring this list. They see this every week."

qa.q: How many pay-later apps did Jomon open?
qa.a: Three pay-later apps.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when Jomon turned the pad towards her?
qa.a: She was shocked and embarrassed, eyes widening, as she saw that the tiny instalments added up to more than her library wages.

qa.q: Why was Jomon's suggestion a sensible next step?
qa.a: It kept her calm and sent her, with a written list, to a qualified college advisor who handles this often, instead of guessing alone.

qa.q: How does Jomon seem to see Zainab's situation?
qa.a: Jomon treats it calmly and without judgement, as a common problem to lay out and take to the right person.

grounding: Shows a young adult who treats no-cost instalments and pay-later offers as free, buys beyond her means, and faces a growing total with late charges.

passage: "Vasudha, I saw you slip that bank envelope into your drawer. I won't ask. Just let old Divyansh from accounts tell you about my twenty-fifth year. I had two credit cards, and when the first bill came, I paid it with the second. Then the second with the first. Every month the hole got deeper and the story got neater. I stopped opening envelopes. I told my wife, Meera, that the bank had made an error. I slept badly, snapped at everyone and jumped whenever the landline rang. One night she found a statement in my scooter box. I expected shouting. She sat down and said, 'How long have you been carrying this alone?' The next week we went to the bank together and asked for a repayment plan. It took three years. If I had spoken in the second month instead of the fourteenth, it would have taken far less."

qa.q: Where did Meera find the statement?
qa.a: In Divyansh's scooter box.

qa.q: What was young Divyansh feeling while hiding the cards?
qa.a: Young Divyansh was anxious and ashamed, sleeping badly, snapping at everyone and jumping at every phone call.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Divyansh's story?
qa.a: Meera finding the statement and asking how long Divyansh had carried it alone, after which they went to the bank together and asked for a repayment plan.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt when she found the statement?
qa.a: Meera was probably hurt by the hiding, but her first reaction was concern, not anger.

grounding: Shows a young earner paying one card with another, growing anxious and hiding it from a spouse until honesty and a repayment plan open a way out.

passage: Amara's phone lit up again during dinner in their small London flat: her mother, then her uncle, then the family group. Her brother's fees were due. Her cousin's wedding in Enugu needed "something from the London one". The roof at home was leaking again. Amara loved them; she was the first to go abroad, and sending money home felt like carrying them with her. But the course she wanted, the one to become a midwife, had been "next year" for three years now. "You went quiet," Alejandro said. "I'm angry," she said, surprised to hear it. "And I feel terrible for being angry." That Sunday she called her mother and said it plainly: she would keep helping with the fees and the roof, not the wedding, and some of her pay would stay in London for the course and for emergencies. There was a long silence on the line. Then her mother said, "You should have told us sooner, my daughter."

qa.q: What did Amara want to train to become?
qa.a: A midwife.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Amara have about the requests from home?
qa.a: She feels real love and duty towards her family, but also anger about her own plans slipping, and then guilt for being angry.

qa.q: Which of Amara's choices is most likely to keep the goodwill alive, and why?
qa.a: Telling her mother openly what she could and couldn't cover, rather than quietly giving until she was bitter, so the family knew where they stood.

qa.q: How might Amara's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: Her mother may be surprised and a little hurt at first, but her words suggest she understands and wishes Amara had spoken earlier.

grounding: Shows a young earner abroad torn between love, duty and resentment over family requests, who sets clear limits and keeps some money aside for her own goals.

passage:
30th, evening
Monthly money check, with tea, same as always. Rent, electricity and phone all went out on the 3rd, automatically, like every month. The savings transfer went on salary day, before I could touch it. So the only real work tonight was reading the spending list: lots of auto rides this month because of the rain, fewer takeaways than last month. Fine.
The one surprise: my laptop charger died on the 18th. Thomas at work said, "Just get a new laptop on the card offer, no-cost EMI, everyone does it." I thought about it for exactly one evening. Then I paid for the charger from the small emergency pot, which will fill back up over the next couple of months.
What I noticed: I didn't panic once. Two years ago a dead charger would have meant a crisis and a card bill. This time it was a single line in the notebook.
Ganga

qa.q: On which date did Ganga's laptop charger die?
qa.a: On the 18th.

qa.q: How does Ganga feel about the charger breaking?
qa.a: Ganga feels calm and steady, noticing with some pride that there was no panic at all.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's habits made the broken charger a small thing?
qa.a: Bills paid automatically on fixed dates, savings moved on salary day, a small emergency pot and a monthly review meant the charger was paid for without borrowing.

qa.q: How might Thomas see Ganga's choice about the laptop offer?
qa.a: Thomas may find it surprising or overly careful, seeing card offers as normal, while to Ganga it was a trap not worth stepping into.

grounding: Illustrates a steady money handler who pays bills on fixed dates, saves first, keeps an emergency reserve, reviews monthly and avoids an easy credit offer.

passage: The science olympiad form had a red warning in capitals: DETAILS CANNOT BE CHANGED AFTER SUBMISSION. Arohi read it three times at the dining table of the Salt Lake flat, and her stomach knotted. Name: she typed it, deleted it, typed it again slowly, then held her school ID card beside the screen and checked every letter. Date of birth: the form wanted the month first. Her birth certificate said 07/03, meaning 7 March, so she had to type 03/07. She almost missed it. "Arnab, is this right?" Her brother leaned over. "Looks fine. Submit." But the form also asked for a school code, and she didn't know it. Guessing felt dangerous. She messaged Mrs Ghosh, the olympiad teacher, and waited, jiggling her knee. Twenty minutes later the reply came with the code. Arohi checked the whole page once more against her ID, pressed Submit, and breathed out properly for the first time that evening.

qa.q: Who did Arohi message about the school code?
qa.a: Mrs Ghosh, the olympiad teacher.

qa.q: How was Arohi feeling while she filled in the form?
qa.a: She was anxious, her stomach knotted by the red warning, and she stayed tense, jiggling her knee, until she finally breathed out after submitting.

qa.q: Which of Arohi's steps protected her from a mistake she couldn't fix?
qa.a: Checking every letter against her school ID, catching the month-first date, and asking Mrs Ghosh for the code instead of guessing.

qa.q: How does Arnab see the form compared with Arohi?
qa.a: Arnab is relaxed and casual, happy to say "Submit", while Arohi feels how hard a wrong detail would be to correct.

grounding: Shows a teenager anxious about errors on an important form who reads carefully, checks against her ID and asks before submitting.

passage:
Farida: I'm at the passport office and I want to cry
Mridul: what happened
Farida: guard sent me to counter B. counter B said get a token from counter A first. counter A said I'm in the wrong line
Farida: and now they want a photocopy of my marksheet, not just the original
Mridul: ugh. the photocopy shop outside?
Farida: queue of 30 people. my slot was 11:30 and it's 11:50
Mridul: ok breathe. ask the help desk if you can still go in after the copy. mine let me
Farida: help desk has no one at it 😩
Mridul: when I went, I called the helpline the day before for the exact list. took originals plus two copies of everything, got there at 8:30
Farida: WHY didn't I ask you yesterday
Farida: ok. copy queue. if they turn me away I'm rebooking the first slot and bringing a whole folder
Mridul: I'll send you my checklist tonight 👍

qa.q: What time was Farida's slot at the passport office?
How is Farida feeling at the passport office?
qa.a: Farida is lost and frustrated, close to tears after being sent between counters and then told a photocopy is missing.

qa.q: What would help Farida avoid a repeat trip?
qa.a: Calling the helpline for the exact list the day before, carrying originals and copies of everything, and arriving early, as Mridul did.

qa.q: How does Mridul respond to Farida's messages?
qa.a: Mridul is sympathetic and practical, calming Farida down, sharing what worked and offering a checklist.

grounding: Shows a young adult lost among counters and conflicting instructions at a government office, and how going early with originals, copies and a checked list saves repeat trips.

passage: On Monday morning, Dolma, manager of the municipal sports complex, called Wasim into her glass office with a folder. "The safety audit came on Saturday. Your lifeguard certificate expired on the 3rd of last month." Wasim laughed, then saw her face. "That can't be. I did the course..." He counted. Two years ago, in the monsoon. The certificate had said valid for two years. He had meant to note the date somewhere and never had. "Until you're recertified, you can coach from the side, but you can't be the lifeguard on duty," Dolma said. That meant Rukhsana would have to cover his evening shifts. Wasim sat in the empty stands afterwards, watching the lanes, embarrassed in a way that felt worse than being told off. That night he booked the next course, then opened the calendar on his phone and added reminders two months before each expiry: the lifeguard card, his scooter insurance, his driving licence.

qa.q: When did Wasim's lifeguard certificate expire?
qa.a: On the 3rd of last month.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel sitting in the empty stands?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, in a way worse than being told off, because the lapse was simply something he had meant to note and never had.

qa.q: What small step will stop this happening again?
qa.a: The calendar reminders he set two months before each expiry, for the lifeguard card, the scooter insurance and the driving licence.

qa.q: How might Rukhsana be affected by the lapse?
qa.a: Rukhsana has to cover Wasim's evening shifts, so a forgotten date becomes extra work and a disrupted routine for someone else.

grounding: Shows an adult who lets a certificate lapse because no reminder existed, and fixes it with simple calendar reminders.

subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]
passage: Rain came down in sheets, the ward office closed at five, and Sangeeta's mother waited outside in an auto, meter running. Sangeeta only needed her mother's name added to the property tax record. Counter three sent her to counter seven. Counter seven sent her back to three. Darshan, a man in a cream shirt, leaned on a pillar. "Madam, I can finish it today. Give me a little something for the babu, he'll sign." Her ears went hot. She wanted to shout, or just pay. Instead she said, "No, thank you," and went back to counter three. "Sir, could you write down which document is missing and the rule that asks for it? Then I'll bring it." The clerk looked up, surprised. Behind him hung a Citizen's Charter board listing time limits and a ground-floor complaint counter. She glanced at it, still polite. He pulled her file over, stamped two pages and said, "Come Friday for the copy."

qa.q: What did Sangeeta need added to the property tax record?
qa.a: Her mother's name.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when Darshan made his offer?
qa.a: She felt angry and helpless, her ears hot, tempted both to shout and to just pay.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta's request to the clerk work better than arguing or paying?
qa.a: Asking politely for the missing document and the rule in writing, with the complaint counter on the wall, made it hard to keep sending her round without a reason.

qa.q: How might the clerk have seen Sangeeta's written request?
qa.a: The clerk seemed caught off guard, perhaps realising she knew her rights and would not pay or give up, and chose to process the file.

grounding: Shows a citizen sent between counters and nudged towards a bribe who stays polite, asks for the rule in writing and points to the complaint route.

passage: I run the cyber café at the corner of our colony, and I see many sons and daughters filling in their parents' forms. Mostly they grab the mouse while the old person sits there like luggage. Last Tuesday was different. Ojas came in with his father, a retired postman, for the senior citizens' bus pass form. Ojas pulled up a second chair but put his father in front of the keyboard. "Papa, this box wants your name exactly as on the ID. You type, I'll read it out." His father typed with one finger, slowly. Twice he hit the wrong key; Ojas only said, "Backspace is this one." When the photo upload failed, Ojas explained what "file too large" meant instead of fixing it silently. It took forty minutes. I can't tell what Ojas felt inside. But when his father clicked Submit, he sat up straight and said, "Done. I did it." I'm Rafiq, eleven years behind this counter, and I wanted to clap.

qa.q: What form did Ojas's father fill in?
qa.a: The senior citizens' bus pass form.

qa.q: What does the father's "Done. I did it" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt proud and capable, sitting up straight because he had done it himself rather than being done for.

qa.q: Which of Ojas's choices protected his father's dignity?
qa.a: Putting his father at the keyboard, reading out the fields, and explaining the upload error instead of quietly taking over.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Ojas's way of helping?
qa.a: Rafiq admires it, contrasting it with the many who treat parents like luggage, and felt like clapping.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult patiently helping an elderly parent with an online form, explaining instead of taking over, so the parent keeps his dignity.
